current_meaning_mnemonic: A stray cat creeps up to the butcher's wooden frame, staring through the gap at two slabs of <radical>meat</radical> hanging inside on their hooks. It leaps at the window and rattles the frame, but the hooks hold fast and the slabs just swing. Peer through that same frame, and all you'll ever see hanging there is <radical>meat</radical>.

Toto the door-to-door turtle sets up shop outside Koichi's konbini, hauling a sample <radical>door</radical> off his shell. Its top panel keeps swinging open on its own, scraping against the sill with every gust. He pitches it as a feature: it never latches, so you're never locked out again. Nobody wants that.

A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> droops so low under its own ripe weight that it finally topples into the <radical>fire</radical> crackling beside the field, sparks jumping off both sides as it catches. Farmers burn what's left of the cut stalks every year, before the frost comes. The smell of burnt grain drifting over bare fields is autumn's real signature.

The panicking duck yanks again, and a second matching pair of <radical>feathers</radical> pops loose, drifting down to land tip to tip on the pond, mirrored just like the first pair. A fisherman nearby mistakes the twin shapes for a floating insect and casts his line right between them. He reels in nothing but two soaked, stuck-together feathers.

At Koichi's konbini the door beeps. A hunched shape stumbles in, head ducked like a pigeon's tucked wing. It lands stiff on the onigiri shelf. Underneath, four skinny stick legs splay out and clatter against the tile like a badly tuned xylophone. The clerk just sighs: it's a <radical>bird</radical>.

On the sports field a <radical>bird</radical> lands stiff-legged on the goalpost. Its stick legs clatter against the metal bar. Its beak cracks open into that same perfect square yawn you already know as a <radical>mouth</radical>. It gapes wider than seems possible, and what echoes clear across the field is a piercing chirp.

Halfway up the mountain trail the steep path suddenly flattens into a clearing. Rows of square rice paddies stack neatly on a thick slab of packed earth. The whole grid sits there through every season without shifting. Hikers stop, catch their breath, and realize they've stumbled straight into a <radical>village</radical>.

At Grandma Kane's shrine the <radical>rain</radical> behind the window freezes mid-fall. Its dashes hang stiff in the glass. Someone drags out the <radical>broom</radical>. Its three bristly prongs sweep the frozen drops into pale drifts over the mossy steps. Even the shrine cats won't leave the bell: it's snow.
